Without any particular planning, we decided that in Seoul, we should try the famous Korean Ginseng Chicken Soup, featuring a small whole chicken (mine was a rare black chicken) stuffed with glutinous rice, ginseng, gingko and dates, in a rich broth cooked for ages. Tosokchon Samgyetang is in a beautiful old building. Koreans don't consider this dish food but medicine, and we didn't consider this meal as just food either, but an interesting cultural experience. Each person has to order their own chicken. Don't bother arguing. And I wasn't crazy about the ginseng liquor, nor the milky rice wine. But it was such a great cultural experience. The flavours were intense and unusual, the broth was really rich, and eating our own chicken took a bit of work: interactive eating is quite fun, really. I would recommend this experience, and this restaurant, to anyone visiting Seoul.

My first ever Korean BBQ, and honestly, what a way to be introduced to it. If you’ve never tried Korean BBQ before, the concept is simple — a grill sits right in the centre of your table, and the food is cooked in front of you. At Daol, the staff take care of all of that for you, which made the whole experience completely relaxed and stress-free. They were attentive, friendly, and genuinely seemed to enjoy making sure we were having a great time. Nothing was too much trouble. The banchan (side dishes) that arrived alongside our meal were a real highlight — varied, flavourful, and the perfect accompaniment to the main event. But the star of the show? The sirloin steak. I don’t say this lightly: it was the best sirloin I have ever tasted. Perfectly cooked, unbelievably moist, and so tender it practically melted in your mouth. The quality of the meat speaks for itself. Whether you’re a Korean BBQ veteran or a complete first-timer like I was, Daol is a must-visit. If you’re heading to Myeongdong, do yourself a favour and make this a priority stop — you won’t regret it.

We always stay at the InterContinental Parnas whenever we visit Seoul, whether for business or leisure. As Diamond Royal Ambassador members, we usually enjoy loyalty benefits such as complimentary breakfast and club lounge access. Although we’re not big fans of breakfast, we usually skip it and enjoy coffee at the lounge instead. During our recent 7-day stay, I decided — for the first time — to try the main breakfast restaurant, Grand Kitchen. I went about 15 minutes before closing, just planning to have a cup of coffee and a couple of boiled eggs, nothing elaborate. Upon arrival, the hostess politely checked my room number, informed the team that I was an Ambassador guest, and led me to a table. She offered coffee or tea and mentioned that the kitchen was serving poached eggs with avocado that morning. Since I love avocado, I simply requested a double portion of avocado without the eggs. She looked confused but said she would check with the kitchen. While waiting, I walked around and admired the impressive breakfast selection. I picked up some eggs and made myself a glass of fresh green juice. However, when I returned to my table, I was shocked to see a plate of avocado that was clearly spoiled—brown, mushy slices that should never have been served to any guest, let alone one at a hotel of this standard. To make things worse, the coffee I had ordered earlier never arrived. I approached the barista section to request a simple black coffee, but the young man informed me that breakfast service had ended and he could no longer make one. This was frustrating, considering I could have easily enjoyed attentive service and unlimited coffee at the club lounge on the 34th floor. Overall, this experience was very disappointing. I understand that it was close to closing time, but that should never justify cold service or food that’s unfit to be served. Guests deserve care and hospitality regardless of the hour. Sadly, this visit left me feeling unwelcome — and I decided not to return to the main breakfast restaurant again.

Me & my cousin visited the restaurant this evening. It was a lovely experience worthy of its Michelin star rating. You are given your own private room that the waitresses gently wait on you. However, if you really wish to enjoy this meal and appreciate how well done it is, you have to have a good understanding of Buddhist culture. I myself am not really familiar with it, so when we went, unfortunately it was a little difficult. First, I have attached a brochure they have at the front of the restaurant that I sadly missed when we came in. It gives a little background behind the naming of the courses and some Buddhist ideals. Second, if you want some of the fancier meals, you have to book in advance, but also let them know three days before that you want those meals. The instructions in the menu are a little unclear, saying “parties more than four, but less than eight”, but if you want those pricier meals, you should book ahead. Thirdly, I think it was interesting to try the foods in different ways. I tried to try each dish individually, with different combos, and in different orders and it was definitely adding to the experience, given that each one yielded a different result. Even if you find the experience a little unpalatable, try to finish every dish because it is very poor in Buddhist culture (and any Michelin star restaurant), to leave food behind. Manjok Ohyang Jokbal is known as one of the 3 best Jokbal brands in Seoul. When we arrived at its front door for lunch, we were surprised to learn that it holds two Michelin Awards; one for 2017 and another for 2018. Jokbal is made from Pork Hock and Foot. The secret of Manjok Ohyang Jokbal is its Ohyang taste. Ohyang in Korean means five spice, which indicates a mixed flavor of various kinds of spices. The main ingredient of Ohyang is Star Anise, a traditional spice having been used for cooking since 3000 years ago first in China. Served with Garlic Sauce, sliced Cabbage and Korean Dumpling Soup, the Ohyang Jokbal is the all-time favorite. The great smell caught us as soon as it was placed on our table. The meat has a moderate salty taste, a little bit sweet, and strong unique spice taste just like five spice. The skin looks quite fat but it is surprisingly not greasy, and really melts in your mouth. Within 15 minutes of arriving, both floors of the two-story restaurant were full business people, tour groups, and just people out for lunch. Pricing for this wonderful meal was inexpensive.

I was by myself and therefore was able to sit at the bar counter which faces to coffee machine and girl who does all the drinks and coffee. Order is pretty simple. Since I went for breakfast/brunch, I chose the 4 options order: I picked smoked salmon, scrambled eggs, avocado and sourdough bread. I also ordered the daily cold-pressed drink which was beets, carrots, apples and lemon. My meal was absolutely delicious. The sourdough bread was so soft inside and crusty on the outside. I had never tasted sourdough bread before and I will definitely make it when I return home from my trip. The avocado was succulent, they seasoned and added some nuts to it, and it so so tasty. One thing I want to write about is the cold-pressed drink, NO SUGAR ADDED, it was the best fruit juice I’ve had during this trip and I don’t even remember having something this delicious. I was sitting right in front of the machine and they definitely use fresh fruits and veggies and do it manually. I should’ve asked for more and more, pretty their forearms would be sore at the end of the day... just so delicious and straight from the fruits and veggies! When I first took a sip, I couldn’t believe how the mix went together so well. I usually don’t give out reviews this good but this tiny restaurant exceeded my expectations. They desire the good reviews and I wish them well in their business. Watching them work while the place was packed and busy was good to see. They still offered excellent service and food, kudos! The drink was 5,500 KRW and the meal 12,000 KRW. It is worth the price IMO. Again, I HIGHLY RECOMMEND this restaurant for breakfast/brunch/lunch/dinner.

If you want to enjoy an exotic culinary experience while dining in a traditional Korean space, I highly recommend this place.

I came here to celebrate my sister’s birthday, and from the moment we arrived it felt festive in all the right ways. The atmosphere is beautiful both outside and indoors, stylish, warm, and thoughtfully designed. The interior blends traditional hanok elements with a contemporary aesthetic, which perfectly reflects the menu: a clever fusion of Korean and European cuisine. The food is ideal for anyone easing their way into Korean flavors, as well as those simply looking to treat themselves to something a little different. Standout dishes for me were the jeon potato pancake to start and the truffle sujebi gnocchi, comforting, creative and full of flavor. For drinks, we tried sikhye, the traditional sweet fermented rice drink, which was refreshing and lightly sweet. The dessert is also a must, they only have one but it reminded me of retro Korean snack with something new added to it. Everything from the food to the ambiance felt well-curated, making it a lovely spot to celebrate or enjoy a relaxed, memorable meal. I loved it and will definitely be bringing my friends next time.

Note: I understood from my Korean friend that the restaurant address I had from most bloggers's sites (19-1 Anguk dong) were the old form of address used in Korea. A long overdue review but had to do one as it left a lasting impression! Stepping into Hue 135 in Itaewon, Korea, is like entering a realm of elegance and sophistication. The restaurant’s modern decor is a perfect blend of chic minimalism and luxurious comfort. Soft, ambient lighting casts a warm glow over the tastefully arranged tables, creating an intimate atmosphere ideal for a romantic dinner or a special celebration. The stylish interior, with its subtle nods to both Western and Korean aesthetics, sets the stage for an exceptional dining experience. Course menu included a sashimi of the day, tartare, chawanmushi, and a trio of meats: charcoal-grilled hanwoo special cuts, nook rubbed hanwoo tenderloin steak, dry aged hanwoo steak (30 days) which were cuts of meats that one wouldn’t be able to get an any ordinary steakhouse. These fine cuts were followed by a savory truffle mushroom steamed rice set and a 48hr based short-rib. The dessert was a play on a korean candy called yuht and Hue135’s own beef jerky - which was crispy and light. Hue 135 is more than just a steak restaurant; it is a fine dining experience that caters to all the senses. The combination of exquisite food, exceptional service, and a luxurious yet inviting atmosphere makes it a standout destination in Itaewon. Whether you are celebrating a special occasion or simply indulging in a night of culinary delight. The steaks are outstanding and every dish that compliments the meat.

The steak was cooked perfectly, as ordered, and the unique taste from the dry-aging process was noticeable. We ate about half of it, and moved on to dessert. Although the set menu included a brownie with ice cream, they graciously allowed us to substitute the Tiramisu, which was delicious. Thought the meal, the service was fantastic. Very attentive waitstaff, without the feeling that they were hovering over the table. Why only four stars? They were out of Caesar Salad, and didn't have sweet vermouth to make a Manhattan. Two issues that are very odd in a NYC based chain steakhouse. Additionally,malt bough the decor and cleanliness of the actual restaurant were fantastic, the entryway stairs smelled like they hadn't been cleaned since the 1970s. Absolutely gross introduction to a fantastic restaurant. Anyways, two small distractions to a fantastic dinner.

A Heavenly Encounter with the Ocean: Lobster and Abalone Pasta Review Some meals don’t just feed you—they stay with you. That was exactly my experience with the best lobster pasta and abalone pasta I’ve ever eaten. Every bite was a love letter to the sea, expertly crafted and passionately plated. Lobster Pasta: The moment the dish hit the table, the aroma of garlic, white wine, and lobster shells made my senses come alive. The lobster was impossibly tender, succulent without a hint of chewiness, nestled in a perfectly balanced sauce—rich but not overwhelming. It clung to al dente linguine in all the right ways. There was a deep, buttery sweetness to the lobster meat, elevated by a touch of chili heat that added just the right kick. This was no ordinary seafood pasta—it was indulgence with soul. Abalone Pasta: And then came the abalone pasta, an experience in elegance. The abalone was sliced just thick enough to showcase its unique texture: firm yet delicate, with a subtle ocean brininess that lingered beautifully. The sauce was a gentle emulsion of olive oil, garlic, and perhaps a whisper of seaweed or fish stock—just enough to enhance without overshadowing. The pasta itself was handmade and silky, providing the perfect canvas for the abalone’s natural umami. Both dishes felt like the ocean had been captured and refined into art. Fresh, luxurious, and balanced—they didn’t try too hard. They didn’t need to. Verdict: These weren’t just pastas. They were moments—slow, flavorful, unforgettable. If I could relive that meal again for the first time, I would.

Most people focus on the fish when it comes to sushi, but the key to a good sushi is getting the balance just right between the rice and the fish. And the rice part is more important than most people give credit. Just ask Jiro Ono of "Jiro Dreams of Sushi." That same dedication to rice is evident at Sushi Hyo. In fact, I don't know if it's true, but I've heard that the owner/chef of the restaurant only uses fresh spring water from the mountains to cook his rice. I've also heard that he has been just as dedicated in procuring the best salt, rice, etc. Perhaps those are the reasons, but Sushi Hyo is hands down the best sushi place in Seoul, but you must sit at the counter to really get the full experience. I've dined numerous times in both the dining room and at the counter and the quality was not quite the same. Maybe it's because the owner prepares most of the sushi at the counter, but the balance between the rice and the fish was perfect.

I don't claim to be a sushi expert, but my reaction to Sushi Hyo is written from the context of having lived in Tokyo for six years. I didn't find the sushi particularly distinguished, especially for the very very high price being charged. But what really bothered me was a lack of grace and no sense of pacing. A Korean friend tipped me off to this great find. It is hidden in one of the back alleys in the Seodaemun section of Seoul, close to the Seodaemun subway station. This old school Korean restaurant specializes in marinated pork and a cooked sour kimchi which is amazing. The boneless pork falls apart with a little pressure from your chopsticks and it is accompanied by a large serving of the very sour cooked kimchi which is a perfect accompaniment. They conveniently supply scissors to cut the kimchi into smaller pieces. Along with the main course comes a nice selection of side dishes which complement the main event. I have had their omelet as well and that is also very tasty. This place is definitely a local's restaurant and not on the tourist radar. Seating is mostly traditional low Korean tables where you sit on the floor but they do have a few western tables in the back. Traditional Korean beverages - soju and beer finish the meal. Also very inexpensive. This is definitely a keeper!

My partner ordered a hamburger with fries. The fries looked and tasted like 'frozen fries": the skinny fries that looked and tasted like MacDonald's fries. The hamburger was okay. Nothing to write hone about. My "Vongole with Agio e Olio" spaghetti was more like spaghetti in soupy sauce. What was wrong? 1. "Aglio e Olio" is a classic garlic and oil Italian dish. Simple but not easy to prepare well. People who ordered it would expect a classic. Same reason you don't call any pasta dish with some cheese and a little pepper "Cacio e Pepe". 2. The sauce in "Aglio e Olio" is an olive oil and pasta water emulsion which is creamy. The dish I had was soupy (see photo). Certainly no emulsion there. The kitchen could have at least boiled down the watery sauce to make it thicker and concentrate the flavor a bit. 3. The name "Vongole .." was again misleading. There were a few small clams (vongole), a few mussels (cozze) and a couple of shrimps (gamberi). Why not call it a seafood pasta with clams, mussels and shrimps ....? The decor was nice though.

Good location and a very imaginative design in a modern setting. Everything about "Pairing Room" is good, but it lacks one essential element of an Italian restaurant - an Italian chef, maitre d' or owner. Any one of these roles could be filled by an Italian and it would take this restaurant to the next level. Not an easy recommendation to follow, understandably, but, without it, there is a ceiling which it will not break through. The staff were extremely pleasant, the service good and the food way above average, without being exceptional. At around 9:00 p.m., I was reminded that the kitchen was about to close. I am not a dessert eater, but do like to finish off an Italian meal with a good espresso and perhaps even a glass of sambuca or grappa. I had not finished by main course at 9:00 p.m. - I arrived back in Seoul quite late - but the waitress politely informed me that at 9:00 p.m., the coffee machine would be switched off! There were at least a dozen people still in the "Pairing Room" at that time, but the cleaning up and shutting down process had already started as we finished our evening there. No good Italian would let that happen. Good value, good food, but for a 5-star rating, it needs a little more Italian, less corporate, approach.

Being an expat and from California, you crave things from back home and burgers are always on the top of the list. I've googled best burgers in Seoul thousands of times and Brooklyn Burger is usually on the top 10. This increased my expectations but I was still a bit skeptical since burgers are a bit trendy these days and everyone is trying to jump on the "handmade" burger band wagon and there are a bunch of "power bloggers" falsely promoting how good this or that burger place is. (I'm from California the land of In-n-Out which has a huge cult following). I went with my gf on a Sunday around 7:30 PM and there were 4 parties already waiting in line. The ambiance is a kind of retro-American-dinerish that didn't fully materialize into full authenticity. Open the door under the bright neon Brooklyn Burger sign and you will be greeted by a full size Star Wars arcade game (it's free to play) and "WWF" folding chairs. I think the chairs were a sign of the main event that was about to take place in my mouth. The wait time was faster than I expected about 15-20 minutes at least faster than my gf turning hangry. We were seated at the counter, which had a gracious line up of several hot sauces, She ordered the Brooklyn Works 7oz with the optional set to add cheese fries (covered in cheese sauce) and a can soda. I went with the Cheese skirt 7oz with sweet potato fries (thin cut) and a can of Dr. Pepper. The patties are cooked "medium-well" by default but can be made to your preference of wellness. The patty was the perfect amount of juiciness and seasoning. The bun to meat to topping ratio was the right size to hold in your hand and bite into without having to cut it with a fork and knife. I hate it when other places pack too much crap and the burger doesn't taste good, it is too big or it is too juicy that it ruins your bun and it falls apart. The cheese skirt is delicious. If you haven't tried the cheese skirt, the best way to describe it would be to imagine bacon cheese, crispy and salty. The cheese fries and sweet potato fries were both good but not to die for. Unfortunately, we didn't order a milk shake which I heard were also really good but a bit high on calories (what would you expect from a nutella milk shake). I think next time we might opt out of the fries and split a shake instead. The staff were very polite, attentive, prompt and spoke English. Total damage: about 35,000 won, totally stuffed and burger craving knocked out.

Thankfully, we stumbled upon a good samaritan who helped us with finding this restaurant. It was a 4-5 block walk from Apgujeong station. It's my first time to be in Seoul and I know that Galbi-jjim (slow cooked braised beef short ribs) is a very special dish in Korea. I had tried it elsewhere and I even know how to make it, but I just had to try it as it is made by a Korean in Korea. And I definitely had to try it in a restaurant recommended by the locals. When asked what size of the dish we preferred, small, medium or large, I said "LARGE". I was just too hungry after having to walk around for 30 minutes just to find the restaurant. When the dish arrived with a pair of tongs and scissors, I just stared at the large pot of beef ribs and wondered how the 3 of us will ever finish it beofre the shop closes. It was as if we ordered a whole cow. Everyone was silent through the meal. All I could hear is the sound of 3 really hungry people enjoying succulent Korean beef short ribs. And yes, we did finish it eventually. I even found myself dipping the bones into the sauce to consume every bit of flavor left from the pot. That good! Hopefully, in my future visits, they'll open a shop somewhere more accessible - in Myeong-dong perhaps. I recommend this to all you carnivores out there.

My wife, two year old daughter, and I ate here for my birthday last week. We arrived fairly early (that's the deal to bring a kid to a place like this) on a weeknight and were the first and only customers in the place for about 20 min. More on that later. We ordered a drink and made our way through the menus and wine list. My Manhattan was excellent and we ordered a half bottle of wine as I had to behave that night! We got the attention of our waitress and ordered dinner. My wife got the French onion soup and I ordered a Caesar Salad. We split the escargot. All of it was fantastic! The escargots were served in the shells and had a great herbed flavor without the bath of garlic butter that makes them so heavy sometimes. My wife's lamb chops and my steak came out next. Everything was cooked absolutely perfectly. Like, perfectly! My steak was a monstrous dry-aged bone in strip and the flavors were everything I had hoped for. We boxed up half of the meal and had a very delicious Tiramisu for dessert. I ate the rest for lunch at work later. The food was exceptional! So, why not five stars? It was tough not to, the food was some of the best I've had anywhere, ever. Here are the details... The service was ok. Our waitress was not very engaged or interested in our experience, but was available and timely. I am fairly certain that this was due to her discomfort with English. I understand, but there's more. We called before dinner to make a reservation and ask if they had a corkage fee (they did, $35) but the woman who answered the phone did not understand any of my questions, and couldn't tell me that. Nor could she take my reservation or transfer the phone to someone who could. I realize we live in Korea, and English is not the primary language. I'm certainly not arrogant enough to demand it be, and we love living in Korea. This brings me to my second minor ding. If you run a restaurant that charges $200 a person, please have an available translator. That corkage fee would have saved my $75 and got me a better wine because, lets face it. This restaurant is exorbitantly priced, by any standard! Peter Lugars? Nope. Craft Steak? Nope. Shoot, I can't name a steakhouse that charges as much as this place and I've been to some of the world's best. Yet they still get 4 stars...because it was that amazingly tasty! I'd go back, but will bring my own bottle of amazing wine.

Oh and they give you business cards that have their address in Korean. This is important because when flagging regular taxis down, a lot don’t speak English, so they won’t take you unless they see something in Korean, like this card. There are black taxis specific for foreigners, but they are not the majority, so this card comes in handy. You’ll see it at concierge. They are the ones who book your taxis. That’s the only difference we saw. At the Sheraton, their staff opened the taxi door & greeted you with happy faces. As soon as you walk in, more staff is greeting you, so much that by the time you leave everyone at the front & at the front desk is your best friend. This isn’t the case at this hotel. No one is jumping up to help you. It’s like they are more timid. Once you approach them, they are ready & willing. No one will greet you at your taxi, but hey the hotel is magical. I have just eaten at this restaurant. It was not my first choice but having endured a 7 hour journey from Jinju that should have taken 4 I was in no mood to trek halfway across Gangnam-gu to find my first choice. The restaurant is situated opposite the Intercontinental COEX where I was staying. Initially I wasn’t sure it was the correct place but the crowds outside and the pig snout seemed to give it away. I was greeted by a guy that I can only describe as looking a bit like Yoda. I mean that in a good way....the kind of guy that guides you through your journey only with more enthusiasm. He explained in broken English that I needed two people but I assured him that although I was one. I would eat for two (having not eaten for over 24 hours). I was going to order more than I did but he told me it was too much for one and so I settled on the pork belly and the glazed pork rib. I was comfortable using the chopsticks and cooking myself having visited Korea several times a year for the past 14 years but he insisted on cooking much to the disdain and disapproval of the ladies clearing tables. At one point he disappeared and one of the ladies came over and turned some of the cuts of meat then told me she was very busy so I should do it myself. There are times when this would annoy me but I just found it funny as I hadn’t asked her to do anything in the first place and was quite in control. The pork belly was good but I have better but the glazed rib was divine. I came close to ordering another but the lady came and whisked away the coals before I could. It would have been pure greed though. Side dishes were lovely and I especially enjoyed the kimchi as it really cut through some of the fattyness of the pork and had a good kick to it. I think had I been served by another person my rating would probably be lower but the gentleman that took care of me was such a nice friendly guy it’s got to be a 5star review. The final bill with two bottles of beer was KRW 50,000 which I thought was good for a city dinner, I pay far more for a similar meal in London or even some of the minor U.K. towns and villages. Next time I’m in Seoul I’m scheduling a dinner here.

I have been a regular diner at Spain Club since it first opened its doors. Over the years, I have enjoyed meals there with just one friend, with large groups of work colleagues and with visiting family members. Each time, it had never disappointed and had always served up good Spanish food and wine in an atmospheric setting. Returning to the Spain Club in Itaewon, I was very disappointed to see how far the standards have fallen. Both the food and the service were mediocre at best and more in keeping with a fast food restaurant than a place with pretensions to offer a quality European dining experience. One of their signature dishes, Gambas al Ajillo used to be my favorite, but now looks pathetic, as the chef has drowned the shrimp in oil with little garlic or paprika. We were still waiting for our drinks to arrive long after all of our dishes had appeared on the table. The staff are in need of a training course on the basics of how food should be served. I'm sorry to see that the management seem to think that they can coast on their old reputation. Adiós Spain Club, I won't be back again.

In fact one of the main reasons to travel to Korea was for us......going out for dining every day. Expectations were high and were mostly - not met! Not so in Gaon. Here we have the restaurant that really deserves its Michelin Stars. Lovely austere design. Tranquility and silence and very beautiful ceramic tableware. Really very special and precious. Such a pleasure. There is however in general a problem with wine pairing or lets better say pairing the food with appropiate drinks. In general most of the restaurants work with wine mostly from european or american wine countries. It is right - spicy food is going well with a good german Riesling and that would be may be the most affordable election. The really good european wines would really break the bank-so the general problem was how to pair excellent food with at least payable lets say „ medium priced“ wines that would go with the food. Thats a challenge! We had a winepairing and it was so lala. Only one drink was indeed from Corea..a corean rice wine. Not the possibilities you have in Japan for sure .The food was incredible and the best we had in our whole vacation. Fleshy prawn with pear, seasoned cucumber and tomato with citrus dressing suberb. Stewed sea cucumber very good. Marinated and steamed crab with squid and kelp just fabulous. Tile fish and clam porridge great. Hay smoked eel marinated with gochujang very delicate. Daily milled rice....and soy bean paste soup - well many people and guests especially from Asia will love that but rice and soy bean paste soup..well not for us. Desserts as usual in Asia a problem for us...if you are accostumed to heartily european delicacies that our beloved patissiers suggest- but -yes an experience and tasting very well but on another and lower level that fab courses of main meal.

It pains me to write this because I had high hopes for this place, especially in the direction it was going right after opening. This bar never really panned out into what it could have been. Popular among the middle aged set and Asian tourists, the money invested in design, quite unfortunately, is wasted on the tiny cocktails and the overall lackluster ambiance. I realize that one is paying almost entirely for the 'experience' of being in this bar, but as someone who has managed a number of successful bars and restaurants, I was and continue to be let down by this establishment, and I've been six times now, just to prove to myself that what I am writing is true. The cocktails are laughably small, while being priced higher than competing hotels, where the drinks are at least properly proportioned. There is always a waiting list to get into this bar, however there is no feasible waiting area, which leaves one to wander around outside the hotel, which is unpleasant in the steamy summers or freezing winters. Once inside, we were seated, and treated to a baby glass of champagne, which is a nice gesture, but the microscopic glass puzzles me every time. They want to make you feel special by giving you a sample of champagne, but it arrives in the smallest glass you've ever seen, like a cheap Costco sample. Once seated, and about 10 minutes after placing a pricey order, the seating staff approached our table and said "Oh, by the way, there is a 10,000 cover fee if you are not a guest". From my experience, it is better to notify patrons of this before they place orders, in fact, before they are actually seated. Lack of training, at it's most obvious. And on the topic of cover charges, let's talk a bit about that for a moment. While seated, we watched countless tourists and locals walk into this place in shorts, tee-shirts, sandals, carrying backpacks etc. It was 11pm at night. Zero dress code in a place where simple cocktails start around $29 USD, and there is a cover charge of $10 per person. It was almost unreal. The management at this place cannot seem to decide if this is a posh bar, or a poolside splash bar in Acapulco. The ambiance is positively ruined by the lack of any sort of screening at the front door. Tons of money poured into the design of this place, the uniforms, the menu etc, and it is full of people in shorts and flip-flops. In short, I can only recommend this bar if you are a middle aged man secretly dating your secretary, and do not wish to be spotted by fashionable people, or if you are a tourist in shorts and flipflops, who doesn't wish to experience the shame of being denied entry at a respectable establishment. Anyone under age 45 should give it a pass regardless.

The restaurant is relatively minimalist in decoration and feels very light and open. Great food, great service and nice view. Whilst not cheap, it's well worth the money. However, other than the beautifully cooked abalone, the thinly sliced, 8 hour marinated, seared beef was delicious -beautifully marbled, prettily presented on top of a spring onion (scallion?) with a small whisper of a gold leaf on the beef on a contrasting dark plate (Deonjang sauce kkurisal). Rolled together with the scallion and the bean paste, it was lovely. The dessert was pretty and seasonal. We were presented with a honied deep fried rice flour cookie (Yakgwa) and an Azalea seasoned rice cake (Jindallae-HwaJeon) served with a cup of a lovely slightly tart maximowiczia tea (Omija-Hwachae) with a cherry blossom floating in it -very nice presentation. I spent eight days eating at various different restaurants in Seoul and most were very good indeed but this is one of two outstanding ones. There were no bad dishes, it was just difficult to decide which dish was best. It was certainly a memorable meal and an experience well worth repeating- lovely!

I went to meet friends at this restaurant they claimed was well known and has been around for a very long time. Walking past trendy and hip eateries like Buzza d' Pizzeria, Root, and Tasting Room, you come across a homely looking house with a sigh proclaiming its presence. Walking in, it feels like Korea or what I imagine Korea in the 1970's before the wealth poured into Seoul. You sit on the floor on linoleum sheeting. The walls are kinda old looking wall paper that festooms the strange assemblage of rooms where they all bleed anonymously with the kitchen as the patrons sit on the floor. The food is primarily korean stew or jigae. But the specialty is "budae jigae" which has its origins from the war when army rations (hot dogs, ground beef, cheese) were incorporated onto the plates of traditional korean fare lprimarily kimchi jigae. The result is a fusion of sorts but it is not an acquired taste. It is simply hearty and flavorful that is immensely enjoyable with a group of friends sitting around a huge pot of "budae jigae". On the menu are sausages. Don't order those. You'll simply pay $10 for a package of boiled Costco hotdogs they usually put in the jigae....unless you really like wieners! Try it and go with an open mind. It is very, very good.

We arrived early evening to awkwardly stand by the counter until a table was free inside. We were given only one menu between 5 people. The menu is short, with a small selection of beef and pork meat platters for the BBQ, one rice option, and a few korean dishes such as bibimbap. The meat is priced per person and is a fair amount, one small portion of meat for one person was around £17 equivalent. The waitress was quite abrupt when demanding we choose what we want to eat, despite us clearly being tourists and not speaking korean, it did not feel very friendly. She did try to answer our questions, but communication was clearly an issue. We eventually ordered two rice bowls (which serve one but was adequate for a few people if you weren't too hungry) and some beef for the grill. The bbq-ing itself is somewhat managed by the staff, although you are given tongs to keep turning the meat. It is very hot, be careful of the flames too, and it does end up very smoky if you are sat indoors. However, as a concept this is quite fun, as you are given control over how you want your food cooked and it is a joint effort for the table to cook the meat - it was quite enjoyable! A selection of sides are brought to you, such as kimchi and other salads and vegetables, although most were very spicy. This is in addition to a salt-pepper mix for the meat. The beef was very delicious, but I was glad I wasn't starving when I entered because other than rice there was not much else to go with the meat, moreso if you can't handle your spice! Overall, very tasty bbq meat and fun bbq-ing experience, but average service and a small menu.

We're a group of 4 and dined there on a week night. Even though we arrived quite late (almost 8pm), we still need to queue for a table: that's alright when everyone follows the rule. Sadly the staff managing the queue was inexperienced (or plain slack), and didn't bother to hand out numbers, if only to eliminate any argument as to who's at top of the queue. As it turned out, a Mandarin-speaking couple with a baby practically jumped the queue & got a table ahead of us (and the couple in front of us)! By which time, we have waited for 15+ minutes, and one of our friend was reasonably upset about the situation. She proceeded to question the staff in question why such unfair practice? Well, what could the staff do now that the quests already taken their seats? It was a dry argument in my view, but nevertheless a reflection on poor management. Another 10 minutes passed before we've allocated a table, and we decided to order a plate of beef, pork & a combo of marinated ribs to share among us. To our surprise the staff who took our order came back & said we've to order 4 dishes as there's 4 of us. OK, our reply was that we'll certainly order more - but only after we sampled each before making a decision on what more to order. The staff mumbled something but decided to leave us alone as the place was still quite busy. 10 more minutes passed, and suddenly another staff appeared and promptly told us our order was 'misplaced' & we need to order again. OK, we placed the same order for the 3 dishes. She looked at us briefly, but didn't say anything. More minutes passed & our dishes arrived. Well, it was virtually lumps of raw meat delivered on plates - the look was unimpressive to say the least, and presentation, what presentation? We almost laughed at how little attention to detail these people placed on presentation - and yes they're busy, but that's no excuse for doing things rough! Having tried Japanese style BBQ before, I must say this so-called gourmet Korean BBQ style is below standard. What about the meat? Having living in the lucky country for quite a while, we're used to quality beef & their various cuts. Well, to be fair, the Korean beef wasn't bad but nowhere near Japanese or Aussie quality. The pork in my view was better (when compared to the beef), and the marinated ribs quite OK but not exciting - considered the price we paid. In the end we decided to order their (signature?) seafood pancake instead of more meat. At KRW15000, the pancake was pleasant but not outstanding, especially so when compared to what we paid for ( half that price! ) at anyone of Myeongdong's famous 'food street' stalls nearby. All in all, we concluded that this so-called gourmet BBQ restaurant is over-rated & over-priced. Considered our unpleasant experience with their unprofessional staff there, I would highly recommend you save your money and GO SOMEWHERE ELSE.

Went as a family with two kids. Once you come out of Wangsimni station, just follow the main road and walk for another less than 10mins. The smell of bbq hits you once you go down the stairs to the restaurant but once you get used to that and the dimness, it was great. We went before 7pm and the restaurant was already nearly full. The tanks were filled to the brim with live clams of all kinds. We were given a plate per table to collect the seafood and honestly it wasn’t a big plate but one plate is typically sufficient to fill up the space on the grill so it was fine. The abalones were obviously the most popular item and they were baby-sized so one mouth per abalone? The scallops and clams were all alive to the extent of spitting out water when we picked them up. Watch them sizzle and pop on the grill but mind not to overcook them which we did for the first batch. Don’t bother with the huge clam as the meat was tough. The smaller ones are lovely. Mind that the oysters need to be wrapped in aluminum foil before grilling but ours didn’t open no matter how long it was on the grill so we gave up on that. Try not to get the tank water on your bare skin. I had some spilt on my arms and it itched after that. Saw many tables with small pots filled with spicy ramen soup and seafood but you will need to pay separately for ramen. Else, just take a pot and fill it with water (available at water dispensers), dump copious amount of clams, and vegetables into it and boil it into a delicious seafood soup to end the meal. In all, a great experience.

When I arrived at the building at about 5:30pm, there was nothing to suggest the presence of a restaurant popular with the locals. When I walked down to the basement I was surprised to see a crowded smoky restaurant. Soon after, there was a crowd at the entrance and by the time we left, the queue stretched all the way up to the street level. Get the big blue plastic bag to seal your bags and coats. The wait staff will give you instructions and off you go for the food. One container for seafood and the other for non seafood. One pail for the empty shells and a small plastic basket for items with extra charges. There are all sorts of shellfish. I find the gigantic clams not delicious. I prefer the smaller ones and of course the abalones. There are also vegetables, other meat, sausage, ramen and rice. Surprisingly there is an extra charge for the rice, The buffet costs KRW25,000 per person. Drinks are not included. Place the empty drink cans or packets into the small plastic basket, bring it to the cashier for payment before you leave. I read a review of this small Mom and Pop-type restaurant, located in a working class neighborhood of Seoul, and decided to check it out for lunch. I arrived around 2 pm and was surprised to see a fair number of people still in the place. The other diners were a mix of young couples and some older people. The menu is limited and written on a sign on the wall, only in Korean. But the main specialty, which I ordered, is jamjatang (potato and pork bone soup.) It is a large bowl of soup with a spicy broth overflowing with pork bones and potatoes and some other vegetables. There will be a small pail where you stack the bones after scraping the meat off of them and into the soup. Sides of white rice (bap) and some kimchis round out the meal. Adding some rice to the soup makes it even more robust and filling. This dish was very good and the restaurant is inexpensive. I think they were a bit surprised to see me in the restaurant as a foreigner, but they were friendly and welcoming. Don't expect fancy decor - its strictly utilitarian. The easiest way to get there is to take the subway to Euljiro 3 ga and go out exit 2. Walk down the street and take the first left turn. Then take the second right turn and you will see the restaurant on the left. From the subway exit to the restaurant you will see lots of tile and plumbing stores. It should take just a couple minutes to get there.

Hoping they would still accept us, I asked if they would, adding we were quite hungry. They still had a couple of customers, so we were accepted. The food was absolutely delicious. On my second time in Seoul, a friend told me about a Portuguese Restaurant in town with Portuguese food and a very good wine cellar. I told her...no, it’s not possible. For my surprise when I reach my hotel I got an email from her saying: I booked a table for you at 08:30 pm. Ok, done 👏🤝 After to trespass the door, I saw a huge smile from Kwon (the owner), a Portuguese flag, beautiful tiles, lots of Portuguese wines and the music was fado...OMG I’m at home! After the first surprise, let’s rock and roll...comes the menu and the wine list...what a surprise, more or less 25 different labels from Douro, Alentejo, Vinho Verde, Dão, Lisboa, handpicked by Chef Kwon. Well, to pair with a very good wine we chose Cod Fish Croquette and a fabulous pork Alentejo style. Everything was perfect...incredible! I know very well the Southeast Asia and I can say that in no other Asian country is there a Portuguese food restaurant like this one. A wonderful kitchen, an exemplary wine cellar and a captivating ambience. Congratulations Chef Kwon, I hope to see you very soon at your place.
